sentences.text: Typothorax was an extinct aetosaur, a pseudosuchian distant relative of modern crocodiles, that lived during the Late Triassic period.
Unlike modern crocodilians, this animal was a herbivore, possessing small, leaf-shaped teeth that were not adapted for eating meat.

Its body was covered in ornamented scutes along the sides and underbelly, along with lateral scutes featuring posteriorly hooked horns, but it lacked the large shoulder spikes seen in some relatives like Desmatosuchus.
Typothorax is unique among aetosaurs for having spiked osteoderms located on the underside of its tail near the cloaca.
While not fully adapted for burrowing, it possessed a digging ability not found in other members of its family.

Fossils have been found in the Chinle Formation of Arizona and the Bull Canyon Formation of New Mexico and Texas, making it one of the first Triassic vertebrates from western North America to be named.
Like all aetosaurs and many primitive crurotarsians, Typothorax had upright hind legs held directly beneath its body.
It was likely a slow-moving animal because its femur was almost equal in length to its lower leg bones.

Researchers believe various features of its forelimbs were adaptations for digging, concluding that while it was not specifically adapted for a fully burrowing lifestyle, it possessed a digging capability that other aetosaurs lacked.
The genus Typothorax was named by Cope in 1875 and is classified within the family Stagonolepididae, belonging to the clade Typothoracinae within the subfamily Aetosaurinae.

Two species of Typothorax are known: T. coccinarum and T. antiquum. However, a 2013 redescription by Parker found the holotype of T. coccinarum too fragmentary to be valid, classifying it as a nomen dubium.
Consequently, Episcoposaurus horridus is considered the next available name for material previously referred to T. coccinarum.

Fossils of Typothorax have been discovered in North America, where the animal lived between 216 and 203 million years ago during the Late Triassic, specifically from the Norian to the Rhaetian stages, between 227.3 and 201.4 million years ago.
To preserve taxonomic stability, researchers suggested petitioning for a neotype for T. coccinarum from well-preserved specimens after the original holotype was deemed too fragmentary.

The distinction between Redondasuchus and Typothorax was supported by the description of a new species, R. rineharti, in 2006, with Heckert and other scientists arguing that Redondasuchus is distinct because its paramedian osteoderms are very flexed, whereas Typothorax's are more gently arched.
